Industry News: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Industry observers note that data centers already use light in networking.
  • Sources indicate that the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Industry observers note that data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

Sources indicate that the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

It has been revealed that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The manufacturer’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” states Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Newly introduced Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Industry observers note that inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

Recent findings suggest that VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How substantial do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also vital to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is at the moment choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.

It has been revealed that instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.

According to recent reports, to accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

Sources indicate that the Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

It has been revealed that lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

It has been revealed that “The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

Sources indicate that the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen states, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The tech giant is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another significant advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

In a recent development, “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” indicates Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” states Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the organization announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

Industry observers note that “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Sources indicate that even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch notes.

Recent findings suggest that the Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

Recent findings suggest that lightSolver’s team is presently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Upcoming claims. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Upcoming, Optalysis.

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

Industry observers note that latest says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

According to recent reports, how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he states. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Claims Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print matter as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”.

Want to take great quality shots, but don't have the dollars to spare for an expensive camera? I've gathered together all my top picks for the best cheap cameras to help you out. I'm Pete, and I head up the photography testing team alongside Tom's Guide's reviews section.

The team and I have put our heads together to help you find the best cheap camera for you. Not sure what (or how) to choose? We can help there too, with loads of tips and tricks for finding a great camera.

There are plenty of options too, from mirrorless cameras to point-and-shoots — just think of your use case, and read our detailed breakdown of each model.

Industry observers note that pete is a Senior Editor at Tom’s Guide, overseeing the site's reviews team and all cameras coverage. He was previously an editor for Canon’s editorial site, and has been a photographer for a decade. Pete loves getting his hands on and rigorously testing the latest mirrorless cameras. He’s also the Tom’s Guide action cameras expert, putting each action cam thoroughly through its paces.

Nikita tests some of the best cameras at Tom's Guide, putting each camera through rigorous testing by pushing battery life to the limit, analyzing build quality and features to determine whether it's good value for money. She's also the in-house instant cameras expert as she has been using instant cameras since 2015, and drones expert as she’s a licensed drone pilot.

Ashley is a reviews writer here at Tom’s Guide and spends her time testing, well, everything! A lifelong photography enthusiast, she has a keen eye for detail. She's also Tom's Guide's resident ring lights expert — whether it’s golden hour selfies (she considers herself a professional selfie-taker!) or getting the best lighting for pictures of her dog, she is always putting lighting and camera gear through its paces.

Recent findings suggest that which type of camera do you need? That's important to figure out before you make a purchase. Here's a rundown of the ones that matter (we've included one of each in this guide).

One-line review: The Canon EOS R100 is the cheapest way to get a new mirrorless interchangeable lens camera (ILC), and its excellent image quality and solid AF make it perfect for budding photographers.

People who want to take photography seriously and have lots of creative control over their shots, whether they’re printing them or sharing them on Instagram. It’s ideal for anyone wanting an upgrade from their smartphone without breaking the bank.

In a recent development, the EOS R100 is about as affordable as mirrorless cameras get, yet still offers the essential perks of a “proper” interchangeable lens camera. It has a 24MP APS-C sensor which produces beautiful photos and 4K video. Combined with Canon’s excellent autofocus and the ability to swap lenses when creativity demands, the EOS R100 will give you everything you need to take Instagram-worthy photos.

✅ Beautiful photos: The EOS R100’s 24MP sensor produces beautiful photos with plenty of fine detail. In testing, we loved the natural colors this camera produces, rendering warm skin tones and vivid landscapes — this is Canon all over.

✅ 4K video: The EOS R100 isn’t a video camera, but will still shoot 4K at cinematic 24p, so if you want to dabble in a bit of video, you can!

✅ Great autofocus: Canon’s autofocus systems are legendary. And while the EOS R100 doesn’t have the brand’s very best AF with multiple detection modes (you’ll need the Canon EOS R50 for a taste of that), it still features human face and eye detection, making it great for portraiture and general use.

Industry observers note that ✅ Plenty of creative flexibility: This is one of the only cameras on the list that’ll let you change lenses (the other is the Pentax KF), which is a big deal. As you grow as a photographer, you can swap lenses to tailor the look and style of your photos.

✅ Solid build: Despite being lightweight and compact, this is a Canon camera, so you can rest assured that it’s built to a high standard and will give you many years of loyal service.

❌ Fixed LCD: The EOS R100 has a fixed LCD, which makes it harder to shoot at odd angles, as you can’t articulate the display to suit. It isn’t a touchscreen either, which means you can’t tap to set focus points.

❌ Limited detection modes: As mentioned above, the EOS R100 only features human AF detection modes, so if you’re after a camera for wildlife photography, we’d recommend something with a more expansive AF system, like the EOS R50.

According to recent reports, the EOS R100 isn’t the most feature-packed camera, but packs in a huge amount of functionality and creative flexibility given its budget price tag. If you want a cheap camera to expand your creative horizons and improve your photography, this is the best one to buy.

It has been revealed that "Simply put, I chose the EOS R100 as it's great at doing the basics and costs very little. What more do you need on a budget?".

See Canon EOS R100 sample images.

One-line review: The Pentax KF is one of the only latest DSLR cameras on the market and is great for budding photographers thanks to its weather sealing, IBIS and great real-world color replication.

This camera is perfect for beginners who want a DSLR to learn the basics on, but which will also grow with them — its IBIS and weather sealing will make it a good camera as you explore more genres and get more creative.

In a recent development, the Pentax KF is the best cheap DSLR because it’s essentially the only entry-level DSLR you can still buy upcoming — making it the cheapest by default. It isn’t the most affordable camera on this list, but its U.S. price (under $600) is very attractive given the feature set. It features weather sealing for shooting in all conditions, IBIS for stabilized handheld shots, and face detection AF to nail portraits every time. It’s difficult to find an interchangeable lens camera with IBIS in this price range.

✅ Strong imaging: The camera has excellent color rendition, strong high ISO performance and did well in our challenging dynamic range testing, too.

✅ IBIS: In testing, we were able to shoot as low as 1/4sec without experiencing any visible shake thanks to the KF’s IBIS, which is rare to find at this price point.

✅ Weather sealing: The camera is weather-sealed, so you can take it out with you on adventures without worrying that it will be damaged if it starts to rain.

✅ Angled LCD screen: The vari-angle LCD screen can flip out and rotate 180º, and is ideal for getting shots at lower angles when using live view.

❌ Heavy: Since this is a DSLR, the camera is much heavier than a mirrorless camera. The KF gets onerous to carry after using it for longer stints.

It has been revealed that ❌ Autofocus can lag: Although the camera’s autofocus is generally effective, it may occasionally experience lag. This is annoying at times when you want immediate autofocus.

❌ Not one for video: The KF only shoots video at 1080p, so it’s not a great camera for vlogging or video, which is a shame given it has effective IBIS.

Recent findings suggest that the Pentax KF is a great camera for budding photographers and provides great value for money. It takes great images and has an effective IBIS system, the vari-angle display is useful for shooting at different angles, and the weather-sealed body means it can go with you everywhere and not get damaged by the elements. It’s an ideal camera to both learn and grow with.

"It’s the only budget DSLR still being made, but it’s ideal for beginners learning the exposure triangle on a budget.".

One line review: The Sony ZV-1F is packed with vlogging-specific features that make content creation easy, and it captures detailed 4K/30P video.

Sources indicate that people who are stepping up from smartphone videography, hobbyists, and vloggers looking to take their video content to the next level. It’s ideal for anyone looking to replace their smartphone as their primary vlogging tool while being on a budget.

The Sony ZV-1F is packed with vlogging-specific features, like Product Showcase and Background Defocus, which are usually found on more expensive models. It’s perfect for on-the-fly content creation and to take traveling, thanks to its compact size. It also shoots lovely 4K/30P video, and its straightforward control scheme makes it extremely easy to use.

✅ Compact and portable: Measuring just 4.15 x 2.36 x 1.82 inches and weighing 0.5lbs, the ZV-1F is highly portable as it slips easily into most pockets, and it’s comfortable to hold with either one or both hands.

✅ Easy to use: With its straightforward control scheme and responsive LCD touchscreen, the ZV-1F is extremely easy to use, making the transition from smartphones to cameras seamless.

✅ Lovely video quality: The ZV-1F shoots 4K/30P video and 1080P footage at 5x slow motion by using 120fps. The results are sharp and detailed, and the camera’s autofocus system works well to keep subjects in focus.

✅ Product Showcase: Product Showcase works extremely well for product unboxing videos and reviews as the ZV-1F focuses on the subject closest to the lens while effectively blurring the background. For non-camera-savvy content creators, it makes it easy to create stylized footage.✅ Great built-in mic: The ZV-1F is fitted with a directional three-way capsule mic which captures crisp and clear audio, helping you create content on the fly even if you don’t have an external microphone.

❌ No IBIS: The ZV-1F doesn’t feature in-body image stabilization, which is fairly common in this price range. Instead, you’ll rely on Sony’s SteadyShot technology for capturing smooth and stable footage.

❌ Poor battery life: A single charge yields 360 shots when the monitor is always-on and 540 shots when Auto Monitor off is set to two seconds. This is much lower compared to the ZV-1F’s rivals.

Industry observers note that the Sony ZV-1F is a fantastic camera for those stepping up from smartphone videography and looking to take their vlogging content to the next level — all while being on a budget. Its ease of use, compact body, great built-in mic and vlogging-specific features make it the best cheap vlogging camera.

"Easy: it's the cheapest way to get advanced vlogging features and make great-looking video content for social and YouTube.".

One-line review: The DJI Osmo Action 4 is a feature-packed professional action camera that's cheaper than ever now that it has been succeeded by a newer model.

People who need a rugged video camera — that means content creators, YouTubers and vloggers, shooting video outdoors, especially if it’s high octane.

It has been revealed that the DJI Osmo Action 4 shoots beautiful 4K at up to 120fps, and while YouTube (and most people's monitors) still max out at 4K, you really don’t need more. It’s waterproof down to 59 feet without a case (you’ll only get better than that with its bigger sibling, the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro) and is built to withstand almost anything the elements can throw at it. It also has a front selfie display for vlogging, and a quick-release magnetic mount for securely attaching and switching between accessories, like selfie sticks.

✅ 4K/120p video: The OA4 shoots beautiful 4K/60p footage, for capturing fast-paced action. If you want slow motion video, it’ll also shoot at up to 120fps in full 4K. It also packs a range of professional features, such as Log recording.

✅ Wireless mic hook up: The OA4 can hook up wirelessly to DJI mics, such as the fantastic DJI Mic 2, giving you professional audio quality with no cables or adapters needed!

Sources indicate that ✅ An oldie but a goodie: The Osmo Action 4 has now been succeeded by the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro, driving the OA4’s price down! You can pick it up for just over $200, which is about as cheap as professional-quality action cams come.

✅ So much ruggedness: The OA4 is waterproof to 59 feet, and is fully equipped to withstand the rigors of the environment.

✅ Front vlogging screen: Thanks to its front screen, the OA4 functions well as a vlogging and selfie camera.

Industry observers note that ❌ No higher than 4K: This camera tops out at 4K. That’ll be plenty enough for most people, but if you’re a pro shooter wanting to oversample 4K, you’ll be out of luck.

Sources indicate that ❌ Stabilization not the best: The OA4’s stabilization is decent, but not as good as the OA5 Pro or GoPro Hero12 Black. That said, it’s much better than other budget brand cameras at similar price points, like the Akaso Brave 8 Lite.

It has been revealed that there's a reason the DJI Osmo Action 4 got the "Best Budget" award on our roundup of the best action cameras. Actually, there are a fair few reasons.

One-line review: Despite its tiny stature and budget price, the DJI Neo is absolutely stuffed to the brim with features and doesn't require FAA registration.

According to recent reports, the DJI Neo is for drone novices or enthusiasts on a budget who are looking to enter the world of drone photography. For the features it offers, this drone is excellent value for money.

The Neo is great for those starting out in drone photography because everything is done automatically — from exposure to ISO. The Neo is capable of shooting 4K video at 30fps and capturing 12MP stills. It has been succeeded by the DJI Neo 2, but that drone is quite a bit pricier, so we still favor the original Neo for this guide.

✅ Easy to fly: You can control the Neo either via the DJI Fly app on a smartphone or the RC-N3 controller, and both ways are straightforward. The RC-N3 comes with two detachable joysticks which are highly responsive and comfortable to use for long hours.

✅ User-friendly app: DJI's app is free to download and easy to use, while also providing lots of functionality and control.

According to recent reports, ✅ Compact and lightweight: The Neo weighs just 4.76 ounces which means you don’t need to obtain a license to fly it (but it’s still worth checking local laws before flying). This also means it’s very easy to travel with.

✅ Smooth 4K footage: The Neo shoots 4K video at 30fps or 1080P at 60fps, which is great for the price. Footage is smooth with plenty of detail, as is panning across a scene. Its f/2.8 aperture also delivers good results in moderately lit conditions.

✅ Very affordable: At under $200, this is one of the cheapest and best drones you can buy.

❌ Short flight time: On a single charge, the Neo has a flight time of just 18 minutes which is about half the time you get with DJI’s other drones. It’s worth investing in the Fly More combo which gives you two spare batteries to bump the total flying time up to 54 minutes.

❌ No obstacle avoidance: Unlike pricier DJI drones, the Neo doesn’t feature smart obstacle avoidance. This means that the drone can’t automatically dodge walls or trees, so you’ll have to be mindful of its position in the air at all times.

The Neo is a beginner-friendly drone that doesn’t cost a fortune, making it the ideal choice for aerial enthusiasts. The ability to capture gorgeous 4K footage and detailed stills, combined with its ease of use and lightweight body, makes the Neo the best cheap drone camera.

When buying a cheap camera, you’re naturally going to have to sacrifice a few things. The latest and greatest cameras simply don’t come cheap. Usually, you’ll either have to accept an older model, or sacrifice features.

However, you absolutely don’t have to sacrifice quality. You can pick up some great cameras for well under $100, and they aren’t just cheap crap. And that’s where we come in! This guide is designed to help you filter out the cameras that are cheap, yet still great quality and built to last.

The specific features you need to look for will depend on what you’re using the camera for. If you want to take really nice photos and grow as a photographer, then you’ll want a camera with a larger sensor, decent megapixel count and good autofocus — that means you’ll need to splash out on a DSLR or mirrorless camera.

Shooting video? You’ll want 4K footage, decent stabilization and the ability to connect external microphones. A vlogging camera is ideal, or an action camera if you’ll be shooting outdoors or in extreme environments. If you’re after sky-high footage, then you’ll want a drone (and yes, you can absolutely pick up great drones without breaking the bank).

Want to print your photos? You have a few options. The high-resolution sensors in mirrorless cameras will yield the best results when printing digital images. If you want the film look, you can go for an instant camera, which will be best for immediate printing and documenting social events, or a film camera, which will produce higher quality prints but requires film to be developed.

In a recent development, if you need a camera for travel, then it’s all about portability. You’ll want something that takes decent photos, but is small enough to fit in a pocket or backpack, and which won’t become a chore when worn around your neck.

Every single camera on this list has been through the Tom’s Guide reviews process, which means they’ve all been thoroughly tested by Tom’s Guide experts. The testing process naturally differs for the different categories of cameras — we test an action camera differently to how we test an instant camera, for example.

However, there are many things all cameras have in common. We always test how sharp the camera optics are, looking for optical distortions and image artefacts. We always evaluate how well images turn out, how detailed they are and the color accuracy of the camera. We take lots of test shots or videos with each camera, enabling us to test autofocus, exposure metering and all the extra features such as AF modes.

In a recent development, naturally, we always evaluate the price of a product, test its build quality, and analyze both how easy the camera is to use and how sensibly it’s laid out. If there’s a smartphone app, we use it and evaluate how many extra features it adds, but also how user-friendly it is. We always evaluate the battery life of cameras, too.

We don’t just list the specs or features of these cameras either, and always analyze whether each of a camera’s features is good or bad, and why — that involves weighing it up against the product’s cost and competition. Throughout each review, we constantly compare each product to its rivals to help you make the most informed purchase. We’ve included links to the individual reviews for each camera within every entry, so you can get the full lowdown on each product if you want to know more.

It has been revealed that why spend money on even a cheap camera when you have your smartphone, right? Won't your phone take pictures just as well?

In a recent development, that depends on the phone and indeed the camera, but generally speaking a decent dedicated camera will be able to take better photos than your smartphone. Phones have small image sensors, as there isn't much space inside a phone case for a large sensor. The iPhone 16 uses a 1/1.29-inch sensor, which is a lot smaller than the APS-C sensor used in the Canon EOS R100. A larger sensor delivers cleaner images in low light. That said, many phones these days feature larger sensors than some cameras, especially compact cameras.

Another factor is optics. Smartphones have to use small lenses — again, as space is a major consideration. Smaller lenses just can't match the sharpness and quality of larger lenses on dedicated cameras, especially those on interchangeable lens cameras (like mirrorless or DSLR bodies).

It has been revealed that and while some smartphones offer manual controls, often these aren't truly manual. You can adjust "aperture" on an iPhone, for instance, but the phone simply applies a software-generated blur to approximate the look of a shallow depth of field at wide apertures. While this looks OK at a glance, study the image closely and you'll see mistakes and things blurred that shouldn't be. This reliance on software is repeated in other areas by your smartphone camera, and generally results in poorer image quality.

It has been revealed that and finally, there's use case. If you want to shoot film photos, or print your photos instantly, you can't do either with a smartphone alone. Using a dedicated camera is often more fun, too! There's something special about the experience of using a camera that smartphones can't quite replicate.

That really depends on the category of camera you need, and the definition of “cheap” changes based on said category. If you want the best image quality or a vlogging camera, you’ll need a mirrorless camera like the EOS R100, and cheap means around the $250-$400 mark. Action cameras, expect to spend around $175 - $200 for a cheap model.

It has been revealed that great instant cameras and compact cameras can easily be found for around the $100 mark, while affordable film cameras can be yours for very little more. If you want a cheap drone, you can expect to spend in the vicinity of $200.

Recent findings suggest that no. Or at least, not until they're sure they want to get into photography. Cheap cameras are a great way to see if you like photography (or shooting video), and whether you really want to put in the time and dedication to learn and gain experience.

It has been revealed that that's not to say you should buy the cheapest camera you can find, though, as there are many terrible cameras out there which are a total waste of money. You should buy a decent camera which will allow you to learn without breaking the bank. And that's where this guide comes in! It will help you choose a cheap camera that's also good quality.

In a recent development, support for storing your driver’s license in Apple Wallet has gradually been expanding across the United States. Today, we have a status revision on when the feature will go live in Connecticut, which Apple has touted as a planned partner since September 2021.

It has been revealed that 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

In a recent development, last week, Connecticut released its own mobile ID app for iPhone on the App Store, but without Apple Wallet support. As spotted by MacRumors, however, the app’s developer notes that Apple Wallet support is “coming soon.”.

While the state and developer haven’t shared any more specific information recently, a press release in May from Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont noted the goal is to expand digital wallet ID support to Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, and Samsung Wallet by August 2027.

According to recent reports, connecticut residents have been waiting a long time for the state to launch Apple Wallet ID support. This is the first notable enhancement we’ve had in a while.

When Apple declared support for storing your driver’s license in Apple Wallet in 2021, the firm touted the following partners:.

So three of Apple’s launch partners have yet to roll out support for Apple Wallet IDs. Kentucky previously unveiled that it planned to launch support sometime in the summer, but it has missed that deadline. Evidence found within Apple’s backend code suggests that Utah support should go live soon.

You can use Apple Wallet IDs at TSA checkpoints, as well as at select businesses and organizations in person, in app, and online. It does not replace your physical license. Here are the full details on acceptance.

Industry observers note that apple Wallet support for IDs expanding to additional states isn’t quite as notable as it used to be. Last year, Apple released a new Digital ID feature that is powered by your US passport. While it’s not your driver’s license, it’s a way to use your iPhone at TSA checkpoints at more than 250 airports in the United States.
