General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our GPT‑6 family of models can design upcoming protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
  • Industry observers note that an internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks.
  • Industry observers note that in lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs revealed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our GPT‑6 family of models can design upcoming protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

Industry observers note that an internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

Industry observers note that in lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs revealed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing upcoming proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

According to recent reports, using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Recent findings suggest that our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

It has been revealed that we ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

Industry observers note that the models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

With our research partner, Onava⁠(opens in a latest window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein highlighted evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

According to recent reports, our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

Recent findings suggest that we gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

Recent findings suggest that to turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab.

It has been revealed that we tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study⁠(opens in a fresh window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.

An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target.

We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose upcoming ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

According to recent reports, for three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.

We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design upcoming sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding.

In a recent development, given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both revealed signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.

The unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

Industry observers note that researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called affinity maturation. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design newly introduced loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.

According to recent reports, we started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design latest sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) revealed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.

We then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) indicated binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

Recent findings suggest that A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.

Recent findings suggest that our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray.

Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a new enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.

Recent findings suggest that we tested our models on 30 challenges from MotifBench⁠(opens in a latest window), including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a motif, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called motif scaffolding.

For each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and ESMFold⁠(opens in a new window) to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.

Industry observers note that in a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.

In a recent development, an internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks.

In motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from CATH⁠(opens in a new window), a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.

Many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.

Sources indicate that we counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.

An internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match.

Many medicines, including aspirin, are small molecules, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called docking. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.

In a recent development, for our first docking test, we used the PoseBusters dataset⁠(opens in a upcoming window), a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.

Industry observers note that in practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds. One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt. We tested this on 179 structures from the Scarpino dataset⁠(opens in a new window), where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in 92% of scored predictions⁠(opens in a new window), and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while DiffDock⁠(opens in a new window) reached 60%.

Sources indicate that an internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple highlights the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures.

Where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we indicated the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.

With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.

It has been revealed that because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.

Each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray highlights the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model.

We can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.

We drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.

Industry observers note that in one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called rank correlation. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.

In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.

Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called TM-score. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.

The biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.

It has been revealed that what if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.

Each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray shows the structure measured in experiments.

Each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures.

It is crucial to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.

In a recent development, our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.

Some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.

Sources indicate that the laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.

This work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.

Find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.

Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.

Industry observers note that design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.

According to recent reports, as we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for fresh medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework⁠ guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.

Recent findings suggest that while lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of fresh biotechnologies and new medicines.

Breaking: From CUDA and Jax to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Andlukyane

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that some time ago, I shared a blog post about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs.
  • The short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder.
  • After optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some time ago, I shared a blog post about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs. Recently, Google released TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for TPUs, and I wanted to see how well it works on the same task: whether a PyTorch-native TPU stack could match my A100 training pipeline and my JAX beam search in speed and solution quality, or maybe even beat them.

The short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder. My initial training port was 1.65x slower than the A100 implementation, while the first TPU beam search was 5.7x slower than its JAX counterpart.

After optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially. Training reached comparable wall-clock performance to the A100, and the optimized TorchTPU beam search became 25% faster per level than JAX on the same eight-chip v6e machine, producing the same total solution length across six test puzzles.

Along the way, the investigation improved the solver itself and resulted in an upstream TorchTPU GitHub issue that led to attention-routing fixes.

The code is available on Kaggle notebooks running on a free TPU v5e-8:.

As in the previous post, the code and the experiments were done by coding agents (Claude Code and Codex): I decided what to port, what to measure, and how to judge the results, and they did the implementation and the profiling.

The CayleyPy Professor Tetraminx competition requires finding the shortest sequence of moves that solves 1000 scrambled puzzles. Formally, it is a shortest-path problem in a Cayley graph (each puzzle state is a node, and each of the 24 possible moves is an edge) with an 88-sticker state.

In a recent development, my solver uses beam search guided by a learned neural heuristic — a 3.4M-parameter PieceTransformer. Instead of treating the 88 stickers individually, it groups them into 50 physical pieces, turns each piece into a token, adds a class token (51 tokens in total), and runs four small transformer layers with eight heads of size 32. At the end, an all-neighbours Q head (a head that predicts, for each of the 24 moves, the distance to solved after that move) outputs 24 numbers. So the beam scores all 24 children of a state with one forward pass on the parent.

For training, the signal is a mix of cheap random walks and exact ground truth:.

On the A100, one epoch takes 142.7 seconds. My best checkpoint is epoch 1500 of a 2000-epoch run, about 80 hours in total.

TorchTPU is not PyTorch/XLA: there is no LazyTensor tracing, no xm.mark_step(), and no xla_device(). Instead, TorchTPU lowers ATen ops directly to StableHLO and runs through PJRT and libtpu (PyTorch’s core ops are translated straight into XLA’s input format and executed by the TPU runtime). Once you import torch, "tpu" works as a device string just like "cuda".

Three rules matter in practice:.

Industry observers note that I ran the first port on a Cloud TPU machine with four v6e chips, using DDP with one process per chip and a global batch of 512, so each epoch saw exactly the same number of samples as on the A100. Before the code could run on the TPU at all, I had to remove four GPU idioms (masked_select in the loss, boolean-mask indexing when expanding labels, 12 .item() metric reads per step, and sampling training anchors on the CPU instead of keeping the 0.19 GB anchor table in TPU memory). This first working version took 234.8 seconds per epoch, 1.65x slower than the A100. I was able to bring it down to 132 seconds with two changes.

It has been revealed that the first win was practically free: turning on fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1). Only the model’s forward and backward pass ran under torch.compile; the rest of the trainer (the random-walk sampler with its 40-iteration loop, label expansion, the loss, and the metrics) ran in eager mode, one op at a time. In default eager mode, that data pipeline took 61.3 ms per step. Wrapping it in torch.compile brought it down to 29.7 ms, while fused eager, which fuses the ops at run time without any code changes, got it to 13.1 ms. The pipeline is many tiny ops, and on this workload they fused better than they compiled; I didn’t profile why, since the cheaper option was also the faster one. Setting that single environment variable dropped the epoch time from 234.8 s to 176.5 s.

Industry observers note that still, 176.5 s was slower than the A100, and the GPU profile didn’t help. On the A100, the input stage and embedding gradient took 67% of the step; on the TPU, the same stage took only 0.96 ms (0.8%), and the model was spending ~90% of its time in attention.

Recent findings suggest that A roofline at the model’s own shapes explained why. A square 8192³ GEMM hits 361 TFLOP/s on one v6e chip, and the model’s QKV and FFN GEMMs hit 212–259 TFLOP/s, while attention ran at 3.0 TFLOP/s. With T = 51 and head_dim = 32, every attention matmul is 51x32x51 on a 128x128 matrix unit (MXU) — roughly 2.5% tile occupancy. Padding head_dim to 128 or T to 64 actually made things slower (0.83x and 0.81x). As a result, attention is about 3% of the model’s FLOPs but about 90% of its time on the TPU.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to keep the same model (for a fair comparison), you need to keep the same shapes and find other improvements. Standard scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) expects (B, H, T, Dh), so the QKV tensor has to be permuted to move the heads to the second dimension. Rewriting attention with torch.einsum keeps the heads in their original dimension and avoids the permutes:.

According to recent reports, the fp32 softmax is there for numerics. On the TPU, the einsum and SDPA versions disagreed by a relative 3.3e-3, so I checked both against a float64 reference on the CPU: both were about 4.6e-3 away from it, because the TPU’s matrix unit uses a single-pass bf16 multiply even for “fp32” matmuls unless you raise torch.tpu.precision. In bf16, keeping only the softmax in fp32 closed the remaining gap between the two versions.

This change was almost rejected. The agent first measured it on the forward pass only, where it looked slower (einsum 5.51 ms vs SDPA 4.56 ms), and discarded it on that basis. Thankfully, I decided to check the full forward+backward pass: the profiler attributed much of the backward-pass overhead to layout conversions around SDPA’s saved tensors, which cost far more than the forward pass saved. Across forward+backward, one layer dropped from 25.14 ms to 14.85 ms (1.69x faster). That pushed the whole epoch down to 132.0 s — 1.08x faster than the A100.

Sources indicate that the most confusing bug was in checkpointing. Saving a checkpoint only from rank 0 is a standard pattern:.

According to recent reports, under fused eager, the tensors in state_dict are still deferred. When rank 0 reads them, it executes a graph that includes this step’s DDP collectives, while the other ranks are already waiting at the next barrier. The checkpoint file would grow to 1.1 MB, then 2.2 MB, and freeze forever while every rank sat busy. The fix is to move the tensors to the CPU on every rank and write the file on one:.

The trap only fires in the mode that gives the speedup, which made it harder to find.

On Kaggle’s free v5e-8 (eight chips, 64 samples per chip), the training notebook run 186 epochs in 7.41 hours, with a median of 142.4 seconds per epoch against the A100’s 144.2 over the same epochs.

Industry observers note that over epochs 177-186, the training loss averaged 15.131 on the v5e-8 and 15.132 on the A100, and top-1 accuracy was 0.488 against 0.483. On exact labels, the TPU checkpoint at epoch 186 is on par with the A100 checkpoint at epoch 200: its best predicted move is truly optimal for 99.0% of states, against 98.9%. The best checkpoint trained eight times longer and is still better.

According to recent reports, with training done, the second half was porting my beam search solver (KhoruzhiiSolver, the CUDA beam searcher from the previous post) to TorchTPU. Training needed targeted fixes; the solver needed a rewrite. It relied on torch.unique for deduplication, boolean-mask indexing, and dynamic tensor shapes (cand.index_select(0, unique_pos[:B])), none of which works well on a TPU.

Sources indicate that so I wrote beam_tpu.py from scratch in pure PyTorch with fixed shapes across every step. Instead of dropping duplicates, I sort candidates by hash, flag adjacent matches, and assign duplicate scores +inf so topk simply never picks them:.

According to recent reports, to share a 1M-wide beam across chips, each chip holds an equal share of the beam slots, and a child’s owner chip is determined by its hash. Every step runs the Q-head forward on local parents, routes children to their owners via all_to_all_single, deduplicates globally on each owner, and runs topk for the next level. States are stored as int8, and the tree bookkeeping stays outside the compiled step so the level counter doesn’t trigger a recompilation.

The search doesn’t go all the way to the solved state: it stops as soon as a beam state appears in the exact depth-6 BFS table (27.8M states), and the table supplies the optimal last six moves. In the first TorchTPU version, this endgame tail (a Zobrist hash and a searchsorted over the table for each level, each ending in .item()) ran as eager ops on the TPU and took ~176 s after a 73 s solve. The JAX driver had always done it in NumPy on the host, so I did the same: identical moves on 3000 checked states, at under a millisecond per state. Running the model over fixed-size chunks inside a single scan didn’t change the step speed, but it kept one copy of the model in the compiled graph instead of one per chunk, shrinking the cached compiled code from 363 to 162 MiB.

I first tested an August pre-release of TorchTPU on six hard scrambles (1M beam, 4x v6e). It matched my JAX kernel on path length (186 vs 185 moves, every path replay-verified) but was 5.7x slower (1973 s vs 345 s). The profile indicated that cross-chip all_to_all cost only 0.6 ms per step, while model inference took ~83% of the time. Then I moved to the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 on Kaggle, and the results were surprising: the gap narrowed to 2.8x per beam level, but quality dropped, with TorchTPU finding 194 moves where JAX reproduced its 185.

It has been revealed that because Kaggle has a long TPU queue, I moved to Cloud TPU v6e to debug the 8 moves lost between the pre-release (186) and 0.2.0 (194). Two things had changed in 0.2.0: torch.topk had reverted from a stable tie-breaking order back to an unstable default, and bf16 attention on sequence lengths that are not a multiple of 128 no longer ran the whole module in fp32 (more on attention below).

Sources indicate that on eight v6e chips, forcing the old low-index tie-breaking in topk took 0.2.0 from 193 moves back to 187, the pre-release’s number there. But why should tie-breaking change path length at all? On four chips, every fixed tie order I tried (lowest index first, highest first, a random shuffle) gave 185 moves; only 0.2.0’s native order gave 188. Something in the beam was turning tie order into path length, and that something was my deduplication.

Because the Q head scores children from the parent, a state reached from two parents arrives as two copies with different scores. My dedup sorted candidates by hash and kept the first copy in each run, and since torch.sort is unstable on both builds, “first” was whichever copy the backend left in front. When 0.2.0 changed the tie order, good states started to disappear because their worse duplicate survived. JAX’s dedup uses a stable argsort on score-sorted buckets, so it keeps the better copy.

Replacing “keep first” with a segment-min over (score, index) (so duplicates always keep their best score) added 0.5% overhead and fixed the issue:.

On ten more puzzles, this fix cut total moves from 319 down to 302, improving seven of them and worsening none.

One regression really was TorchTPU’s: on the same chips, 0.2.0 ran a beam level 1.7x slower than the pre-release. Timing each piece of a level separately highlighted that everything except attention was as fast or faster in 0.2.0. The cause was routing: 0.2.0 sends short attention shapes to its Flash attention kernel, which pads the 51-token sequence to a 128-token tile, so 84% of each score tile is padding. Turning Flash off with torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp(False) puts attention back on the plain XLA path (yes, .cuda. — TorchTPU respects PyTorch’s standard SDPA backend switches, which live under torch.backends.cuda):.

According to recent reports, with Flash off, a full beam level is 4x faster than with 0.2.0’s default and 2.4x faster than the pre-release. The 2026-11-04 nightly, which already routes short sequences away from Flash, is as fast as the workaround.

Industry observers note that two things hid this at first. The --fp32-attn arm that I added to test attention precision still went through Flash, so it only made things slower. And PyTorch’s AOTAutograd cache is keyed on the graph, not on the attention backend flag, so a second process quietly reused the Flash-compiled graph and reported identical times until each run got its own cache directory.

According to recent reports, my agent wrote up the measurements and reported the matter to the TorchTPU repository with a Colab reproduction and a table of attention timings across head sizes and sequence lengths. It turned out that the short-sequence fix had already landed on main three days after 0.2.0 was tagged, but it hadn’t been released. The report also noted that a newer routing rule on main would make some 128–256-token shapes slower. The TorchTPU team picked it up, merged a series of attention-routing fixes, and closed the issue on November 21.

Milliseconds per SDPA call on one TPU v6e chip, TorchTPU 0.2.0 · lower is better.

With the dedup fixed and Flash turned off, I reran the comparison on one eight-chip v6e machine with the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 and JAX 0.11.0 (the version in Kaggle’s TPU image).

TorchTPU now runs a beam level 1.25x faster than JAX with the same quality.

Industry observers note that on Kaggle’s v5e-8, the picture is closer. TorchTPU with Flash off is still about 10% faster per beam level, but the median scramble takes slightly longer (49.9 vs 48.7 s), because it checks the hit flag only every four levels and runs extra levels, and it found one move more (186 vs 185):.

In a recent development, JAX remains my main beam search solution for now as I have yet to run TorchTPU on a wider beam. And the investigations helped push the JAX kernel further: bounding temporary buffers reduced the compile-time memory for a 128M beam from 39.5 to 12 GiB per chip, and a 256M-state beam works on eight v6e chips.

I started this experiment to see whether TorchTPU could replace my A100 + JAX setup, and on this task it can: the same model trains at the A100’s speed or slightly faster, and the beam search matches JAX on quality and is a bit faster per level.

However, a native PyTorch API does not eliminate the need for hardware-aware engineering. Static shapes, deferred execution, tensor layouts, compilation caching, and kernel selection all mattered considerably. Optimizations that helped training did not necessarily help inference, and seemingly minor changes in backend behaviour exposed a latent bug in my search algorithm.

The migration also improved both implementations: fixing deduplication reduced solution lengths, the attention investigation contributed to upstream TorchTPU improvements, and revisiting memory management enabled larger beams in JAX.

More broadly, this project demonstrated how AI coding agents can participate in experimental engineering rather than simply code generation. Claude Code and Codex implemented alternative approaches, profiled execution, constructed controlled experiments, investigated regressions, and prepared reproducible bug reports. My role was to formulate hypotheses, choose meaningful metrics, question misleading measurements, and decide which trade-offs were acceptable.

Gödel Enigma

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Helsinki

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gödel's solitary work was the single most important factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine.
  • The development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work.
  • Industry observers note that deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gödel's solitary work was the single most important factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine. His work led to precise notions of algorithmic computability from which a direct path leads to the first theoretical ideas of a computer in the work of Alan Turing in 1936 and John von Neumann some years later.

The development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work. He published in 1967 a collection of original papers under the title From Frege to Gödel: The Development of Mathematical Logic 1879-1931. There was, however, no attempt at organised historical work with the sources. Such detailed work is still in a very early state and crucial sources for the development of logic remain unexplored.

Industry observers note that deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered. Comparison to a parallel and partly overlapping development is illuminating. Quantum mechanics, as well as foundations of mathematics, received a decisive impetus around the year 1900, with Planck's discovery of the quantum of action, and the discovery of Russell's paradox and Hilbert's idea of formalisation. All of these developments led to a well-established theoretical account by the early 1930s, right before the Nazi takeover in Germany: quantum mechanics in the second part of the 1920s in the work of the Göttingers Heisenberg and Born, logic and foundations with the full development of first-order logic by the early 1930s by the Göttingers Hilbert, Bernays, and Gentzen, assisted mainly by Gödel's striking discoveries.

Historical work on the development of quantum mechanics began in the 1960s in a massive effort in which every conceivable source was unearthed and made available in several hundred microfilm reels, the Archive for the History of Quantum Physics.

Sources indicate that sadly, nothing of this kind was ever done with logic and foundations. Our present information society owes a part of its existence to a well-hidden but essential line of development. There are several thousand pages of notes by Gödel waiting to be studied, written in Similarly, extensive notes for lecture courses during the crucial years, written by Paul Bernays, the central driving force in foundational study around 1930, as well as over five thousand contemporaneous letters exist in the Bernays archive. These have been exploited only sporadically. The fate of many other sources, such as the papers of Gerhard Gentzen and Rose Rand, has been similar.

The main aims of our project are twofold:.

Understanding Gödel's unpublished papers requires a combination of mastery of the logical details and the application of professional standards of historical-foundational research to the source material, which, in addition, is only accessible to a reader trained in stenographic writing. So far, much of this work remains to be done. There are two exceptions: the transcription of Gödel's so-called "Zilsel lecture" in Vienna in January 1938 and his Göttingen lecture on the consistency of the continuum hypothesis of December 1939, both published in the third volume of Gödel's Collected Works. Both of these texts were lecture notes, relatively finished in comparison to the private notes. More recently, much effort has been dedicated to producing transcriptions of Gödel's philosophical notebooks that he called "Max Phil," or Philosophical Maxims, in order to better understand Gödel the philosopher. Our project will provide ample material for future generations of philosophers and logicians to complement the picture given by the Philosophical Maxims as well as other works of Gödel's published so far.

The project consists of theoretically oriented basic research. It uses special methods for the study of mostly unpublished primary sources, the contemporary methods of logic and foundational study to aid in their interpretation, up-to-date formal methods for the development of research themes suggested by the sources, and scholarly methodological standards of historical-foundational research.

The main sources comprise a number of series of notebooks, all written in shorthand and logical symbolism, left virtually untouched except for the Max Phil series:.

Gödel's notebooks have some overlap in themes, ideas and results that are presented in Max Phil or Resultate Grundlagen often appearing in less finished form in the Arbeitshefte, to give an example. Gödel was meticulous about keeping his notebooks, and they contain detailed lists of contents from which we can infer that he did reread them. There is a separate list of "Progress" entries, in which he summed both his achievements and objectives in numbered points in the Arbeitshefte.

10 stocks we like better than Microsoft ›.

Industry observers note that there has been a lot of talk surrounding Nvidia over the past few days, and rightfully so, amid serious allegations at the CEO level and potential company misconduct in the getting around U.S. export controls. Other companies have also been in the news such as Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) and its blockbuster initial public offering.

Recent findings suggest that however, one that has flown under the radar is Microsoft (MSFT +0.74%). When the market has a bearish mindset, staying under the radar as a company is normally a good idea, but a company can only keep so much of a low profile when it's the second-largest in the world by market capitalization.

But is Microsoft a good buy today? Or should the market be worried about it too? After all, it hit a fresh all-time high just days ago.

Recent findings suggest that the best companies to compare Microsoft to are Alphabet (GOOG -1.05%) (GOOGL -1.08%) and Amazon (AMZN -1.21%). These two may not seem like great comparisons on the surface, but they are all approaching AI in a similar manner: Investing in outside companies and building out computing power. All three of these companies have significant investments in AI labs to give them exposure to the companies pioneering AI technology.

While Alphabet and Amazon own a massive amount of Anthropic (about 30% combined), Microsoft owns nearly the same amount of OpenAI, its primary competitor. While OpenAI isn't public yet, it will likely become so in the near future, and is likely keeping an eye on how successful Anthropic is on the public markets. So, Microsoft's payday for its OpenAI investment will need to wait, which may not be a bad thing.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

The other area these three compete heavily in is cloud computing. AI firms don't have the resources to build out an extensive data center network to power their workloads. So, they choose to rent it from providers like Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud. All three companies have seen their backlog explode from massive AI computing demand, and the backlog totals are in the hundreds of billions for each manufacturer. As a result, each company is spending heavily to build out its computing capacity.

According to recent reports, however, Microsoft is being less aggressive, which the market respects. This year, both Amazon and Alphabet initiative to spend at least $200 billion on data center capital expenditures. Microsoft only looks to spend $170 billion. While this may sound like it's falling behind, the reality is that Microsoft isn't stretching itself thin.

MSFT Free Cash Flow (Quarterly) data by YCharts.

It has been revealed that microsoft has maintained strong free cash flow, meaning that it's still sending cash to the bottom line. Amazon and Alphabet have dipped into negative territory, meaning they are either burning through cash reserves to fund operations or taking out loans. Both of these two activities aren't favorable in the market's eyes. This could lead to Microsoft being viewed more favorably, but it could cost it some market share in the end if it isn't aggressive enough.

The market normally takes a short-term view for situations like this, which is why Microsoft's stock is viewed favorably. But does that make it a smart buy now?

It has been revealed that microsoft is already in its fiscal 2027, ending June 30. So comparing forward earnings price tags is a bit difficult to its peers. But at 25 times forward earnings, Microsoft is neither expensive nor cheap.

MSFT PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

Amazon is nearly in line with Microsoft's valuation at 24.5 times fiscal 2027 earnings estimates, but Alphabet is far cheaper at 18 times next year's earnings.

GOOG PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

That's a substantial mismatch, and could point to Alphabet being a smarter buy than Microsoft, especially if it can steal some of its cloud computing market share.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft is staying conservative in its spending. We'll see if it costs them, but as of right now, I'd say Microsoft is an OK stock to buy. It will likely beat the market, but won't do it by much due to its current price tag.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

Say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Industry observers note that swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

The revision follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

Applied Materials vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 24, 2026 at 2:30PM EST.
  • Sources indicate that as chip demand evolves, investors must decide between Applied Materials (AMAT -6.66%) and Intel (INTC -8.15%).
  • Applied Materials provides the essential machinery used to fabricate advanced electronics, while Intel designs and manufactures the chips that power computers and data centers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 24, 2026 at 2:30PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Applied Materials ›.

Sources indicate that as chip demand evolves, investors must decide between Applied Materials (AMAT -6.66%) and Intel (INTC -8.15%). Both play vital roles in the global tech ecosystem but at the moment travel very different financial paths.

Applied Materials provides the essential machinery used to fabricate advanced electronics, while Intel designs and manufactures the chips that power computers and data centers. Comparing them highlights the choice between a steady equipment leader and a legacy manufacturer in the midst of a massive structural turnaround.

Applied Materials provides specialized equipment and software for the fabrication of semiconductors and advanced displays. It serves a global customer base including logic, DRAM, and NAND memory manufacturers. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as two specific customers accounted for roughly 19% and 15% of net revenue in the latest annual report.

In a recent development, in the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached about $34.4 billion, representing growth of approximately 21.4% compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was about $10.1 billion, a significant increase from the roughly $7.0 billion reported in the previous year. This growth highlights the ongoing demand for sophisticated production tools among semiconductor stocks.

Recent findings suggest that as of its October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x. This ratio compares total debt to the value of shareholder equity, measuring how much a company relies on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a firm's ability to pay off its short-term obligations using assets it can convert to cash within a year, is roughly 2.3x. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow was approximately $6.2 billion.

Intel designs and manufactures processors and accelerators for cloud, enterprise, and PC markets. The manufacturer is right now pursuing an IDM 2.0 strategy, which involves expanding its own manufacturing capacity to serve external third-party customers through its foundry segment. Its three largest customers are highly concentrated, accounting for approximately 43% of net revenue in its latest annual report.

Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached about $59.9 billion, a growth of roughly 12.1% over the prior twelve-month period. Despite the rise in sales, the company reported a net loss of around $12.0 billion. This loss reflects the immense costs associated with Intel's efforts to modernize its fabrication facilities and regain a competitive edge in processor architecture.

In a recent development, as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.4x. The current ratio stands at roughly 2.0x, indicating a solid ability to cover near-term liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was a negative $4.9 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 25.1% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Applied Materials faces risks from the highly cyclical nature of the semiconductor industry and significant geographic concentration in markets like China and Taiwan. The manufacturer relies heavily on export licenses for sales to China and remains vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and trade restrictions. It also manages ongoing regulatory scrutiny, including a $252 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Commerce in 2026 regarding export compliance.

Intel faces intense competitive threats in its product and foundry segments from rivals such as Nvidia Corp. (NVDA -5.86%) and other major fabricators. Financial pressures have led the organization to cancel facility projects in several countries, including Germany and Israel. It also carries risks related to its reliance on third-party lithography tools and ongoing shareholder litigation concerning its financial disclosures and demand in the PC market.

Intel appears cheaper based on sales, but Applied Materials carries a significantly lower multiple relative to its future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Intel is pressing on with its plan to revive its business. In the spring it unveiled a partnership with Space Exploration Technologies Inc. (SPCX -5.65%) and Tesla Inc. (TSLA -0.20%) to build Terafab, a massive AI chip-making plant aiming to produce as many as 200 billion AI chips a year. Intel is providing its foundry expertise and its 14A process, an effort to produce 1.4-nanometer chips it announced two years ago and is still developing.

Also this year, Intel signed a deal with Nvidia to help build a newly introduced AI GPU called Crescent Island that can work in tandem with Nvidia's Blackwell AI chips, and agreed to help develop an AI-centric chip for the Google division of Alphabet Inc. (GOOG -1.05%), too. Last year, the company raised investments from the U.S. government and SoftBank to improve its capital position.

Recent findings suggest that all that has generated some optimism on Wall Street. For fiscal 2026, sales are seen rising 17% to $61.7 billion, though a large $11 billion net loss is projected, reflecting the cost of expanding its U.S. foundries.

According to recent reports, applied Materials, meanwhile, is the largest supplier in the world of wafer fabrication equipment for semiconductors. Its wide slate of offerings in chip manufacturing gives it inroads with customers by selling integrated solutions across technologies, making it harder for competitors to dislodge it. The business posted a larger-than-expected rise in sales and income for full year 2026, reported earlier this month. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

In a recent development, once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

This post is sponsored by PITAKA.

Plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA says the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

Sources indicate that if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

Industry observers note that PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Industry observers note that spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:.

According to recent reports, buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

If you're anything like me, then you tend to carry a lot of tech with you when you travel. You're supposed to be getting away from it all, not packing all your electronics into the nearest suitcase.

However, there are plenty of gadgets out there that you should aim to take with you on every trip, especially if you're going to be spending multiple hours inside a plane.

The good news is that Black Friday sales have knocked down their prices so, regardless of whether you have any trips planned, now is the perfect time to pick them up at a discount.

Here are 11 of the best Black Friday Travel accessory deals available now.

What if you didn't have to plug your charger into a cheap travel adapter, because the charger itself was an adapter? That's the idea behind Anker's Universal charger, which offers 100W charging speeds regardless of whether you're using U.S., U.K., or EU power outlets. Sadly Australia is not included.

The adapter comes with three USB-C ports, two of which can offer up to 100W charging, as well as a single USB-A port. There's also a handy screen on the front to show you how much power is actually being beamed to all your devices.

Recent findings suggest that I'm a massive fan of magnetic power banks, since they snap onto the back of your phone and wirelessly charge without any pesky cables getting in the way. This MagGo power bank from Anker supports 15W wireless charging and offers up to 10,000 mAh of battery capacity — enough to recharge most flagship phones twice or more. There's also a stand on the back so you can prop up your phone and keep a clear view of the screen while charging. That is especially useful for airplane tray tables, assuming your airline allows you to use portable battery packs on board.

A 25W MagGo variant is also on sale at Amazon for $85 this Black Friday.

Industry observers note that apple's AirTags are the ideal option for iPhone users to track their luggage, since the Find My network uses nearby iPhones and iPads to ping the Tag's location — letting you know whether your bags made it or not. Precision Finding also means you can hunt it down in the airport, should it not appear on the carousel.

Recent findings suggest that airTags can only be tracked by Apple devices, so Android people will need to use an equivalent product that works with the Google Find Hub. Luckily the Moto Tag is also on sale for $18, and includes Ultrawideband support for more accurate tracking.

These days, there are plenty of modern aircraft that feature Bluetooth, which lets you connect your own wireless headphones or earbuds to inflight entertainment systems. That's not always the case, and the AirFly means you can avoid resorting to wired headphones. Just plug into a 3.5mm audio jack, pair to your earbuds, and you're good to go.

The best part is it doesn't just work with planes, you can also use it with just about any device with 3.5mm output — including games consoles, gym equipment and so on.

Apple's AirPods Pro 3 are among the best noise-cancelling earbuds, and that makes them perfect for noisy environments like planes, trains, airports and so on. Plus there's the transparency mode that lets you listen to key announcements without having to take your buds out first.

According to recent reports, the buds have eight hours of battery with ANC switched on and a total of 24 hours with a fully-charged case. They're also IP67 water and dust resistant, which should help to keep them safe from brief dips in hotel pools or any other water you may encounter.

Recent findings suggest that charge all your gadgets in one go with this helpful folding wireless charging stand from uGreen. It features 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging for phones, alongside pads for earbuds and a dedicated Apple Watch charger. It also comes with a compact 45W charging brick.

Recent findings suggest that those of you that don't have Apple Watches, or would rather spend a bit less, can enjoy uGreen's 2-in-1 variant for $28. This offers the same 25W charging for phones, as well as a second pad for earbuds and other devices. But there's no watch charger, nor does it come bundled with a power brick.

You may want to enjoy whatever media you've loaded onto your phone during your flight, but holding onto it for several hours is pretty burdensome. You can use the tray tables, but that isn't always convenient, and you need to stow them during takeoff and landing. The solution? A stand that clips onto the seat in front and holds your phone in place for the duration of the journey.

It has been revealed that the downside is that this is limited to devices under 4-inches in width, which means they're unsuitable for tablets. If you strategy on using a tablet or iPad, you'll need to pick up the larger option for $15.

The fastest charging phones all rely on cables with two USB-C plugs, but the world hasn't really got the memo. Whether you're on a plane, bus or train, odds are they only have USB-A ports for charging — which is basically useless for a USB-C cable. It doesn't help that airlines are banning people from using their own battery packs.

Industry observers note that you could carry two sets of charging cables to cover all your bases, or you could buy an adapter set instead. This bundle has four adapters, two for converting USB-C to USB-A and another two for doing the exact opposite. So, regardless of the cables you have to hand, these should cover you for every eventuality.

As much as you can load up a phone or tablet with content before you travel, nothing quite beats console-level quality on the go. That's where the Nintendo Switch 2 comes in, and Black Friday is one of the few times you can save some money on the console and its bundles.
