Breaking: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greynoise

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure.
  • In a recent development, we witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created.
  • The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.

In a recent development, we witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.

Example POST to loginSrp1 and response.

Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested.

It has been revealed that 2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would glitch commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.

Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.

Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.

The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.

Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant.

They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.

According to recent reports, 2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.

The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.

Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.

According to recent reports, between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor debuted over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.

The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.

2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.

Excerpt from exploit.py -  This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.

2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.

Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.

2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and debuted pull_.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.

Excerpt from pull_.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.

2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.

2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.

2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.

According to recent reports, 2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.

Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.

All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.

Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt.

One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.

After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.

It has been revealed that 2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.

Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

According to recent reports, with AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

Recent findings suggest that this expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

In a recent development, when you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

In a recent development, with AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

Industry observers note that I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the latest speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that owners are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Industry observers note that have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.

Latest Update: Working with AI

⏱️ ~37 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, how are businesses across the economy adopting AI?
  • It has been revealed that the use of LLMs has exploded across the economy.
  • According to recent reports, an employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory.

In a recent development, how are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:.

It has been revealed that the use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange latest collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”.

According to recent reports, an employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”.

Sources indicate that A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a latest workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.

Recent findings suggest that these three firms applied the same technology in the same industry but in different ways. The first firm automated a workflow, creating efficiency gains but risking job displacement for the mail clerks. For the second, bottlenecks to adoption and effective implementation prevented job displacement but also blunted productivity gains that would benefit the firm. The third reorganized work without eliminating any jobs, because effective use of the technology required redeploying employees toward new tasks. The firm redesigned roles to maintain human expertise as a complement to increasingly capable AI models.

In a recent development, in this article, we explore the connections between AI-driven value and work reorganization through 66 face-to-face interviews conducted across 58 companies in the US, all of which are in the midst of adopting AI. We interviewed executives, managers, and individual contributors. We talked to employees at AI-native startups and 100-year-old businesses. We interviewed people at manufacturers and tech companies. We spoke with structural engineers, dentists, and accountants; employees at hedge funds, law firms, and private equity firms; a property manager, a trucking company, and a publisher. They’re all Anthropic customers, but many also use other AI tools. They were selected for this study because of their range across industry, size, and AI usage, though they are not a random or systematically representative sample.

Industry observers note that as in other qualitative research, we present stories and a framework to organize them, with the expectation that follow-up quantitative research can test these ideas further. The interviews were done anonymously, both for the interviewees and their companies. Any names in the report are pseudonyms.

Industry observers note that in our interviews, we gained insight into how AI has become embedded in businesses across the economy. Some of the AI agents we heard about are sending faxes back and forth, as doctors’ offices refer and intake patients. Other agents are giving advice to technicians when an X-ray machine breaks, and still others are then marking up the X-rays to help patients better understand them. Agents are reading property deeds from the 1800s and working out delivery routes for gaming machines. Recently, an AI agent analyzed a manufacturer’s organizational chart and suggested departments where the company could add headcount: “Three heads here, we need to add two there, zero here.”.

According to recent reports, mostly, agents are writing code. Interviewees described 100 pieces of software that they wrote with AI in enough detail that we could categorize them. Eighty percent of this software automated previously manual work, like spreadsheet-based financial updates or taking meeting notes. Another 20% replaced existing software, often previously purchased from outside vendors. Agents are building apps for private parking enforcement, 401(k) audits, and trademark checks for upcoming product names. They are making dashboards to track portfolio companies, equipment repairs, and debt collectors’ phone calls.

According to recent reports, how have human organizations harnessed these new assistants? We use our interviews to explore several aspects of these deployments. We begin by estimating how much value interviewees ascribe to AI deployments and relate that to a measure of how much organizational change they required to implement. Figure 1 plots nearly 300 AI applications that interviewees discussed in detail. We define an application as a specific AI use case in a specific firm. We coded discussions of each application according to the value interviewees attributed to it and the extent to which the organization had to make significant organizational changes to accommodate it. These value assessments are primarily qualitative descriptions on the part of interviewees, not typically based on A/B tests or other quantitative assessments.1.

Sources indicate that figure 1 demonstrates that many light-touch AI applications can fit into an existing organizational structure, like ad hoc data analysis or slide deck design. However, many of the simplest applications were rated as relatively low value by the employees who described them. Higher-value deployments tend to require changes to processes, like AI review of every code commit, or roles, like a marketing manager who edits skill.mds containing branding guidelines instead of designing individual documents.

In a recent development, several interviewees described AI adoption as essentially a challenge of organizational change: flattening organizations, shifting reporting lines, or dropping functions. At one firm, for example, executives decided that junior analysts were no longer necessary because executives could complete their own SQL queries. As one accountant put it, “It’s a combination of process re-engineering and systematic discipline.”.

In a recent development, there are several reasons why the most valuable applications led to significant organizational change. In some cases, the AI applications required a structural change in order to be successful, such as when a policy had to be clarified so that AI agents could rigorously apply it in an assessment workflow. In other cases, initial success spurred excitement about making larger organizational changes to further harness AI. In others, the success of using AI forced downstream changes. One commercial real estate firm saw its staff start sending out client-facing documents themselves. But this meant they had violated company rules that asked employees to route external materials through the marketing department. As an IT director explained, “That’s good because, hey, we got another client. That’s bad because our standard operating procedures are starting to fall apart.” These stories echo academic research that highlights that organizational change is necessary to derive value from transformative technologies.

Next, we studied what, exactly, value means in the context of AI adoption. Figure 2 demonstrates that interviewees described most AI applications as adding value by increasing a firm’s output rather than cutting costs. Around half of the applications that increased output were due to AI accelerating or expanding existing work. The other half were the result of AI improving the quality of products and services or creating fresh products altogether. For instance, a medical group improved service quality by using AI to give patients an up-front estimate of after-insurance costs. A commercial real estate manager mocked up vacant units for potential tenants with their own branding (“Here’s what your sandwich place would look like in this space”). A dental tech giant introduced an after-hours AI answering service, so patients’ midnight calls no longer went to voicemail.

In one-tenth of the use cases laid out in Figure 2, value was captured directly by employees, who were either doing more enjoyable work or were doing less work altogether. One manager described how bringing AI into his construction firm meant that “work can be a joy again instead of a difficult, painful thing.” Senior engineers at an engineering consultancy described being thrilled to be free of tedious standards reconciliation work.

Industry observers note that this sentiment was particularly common in cases where AI sped up peripheral tasks that were distracting to experts, like making pitch decks for product developers or preparing CRM reports for sales representatives. An employee at one construction materials firm remarked they appreciated a whole series of small, personal automations that were “changing my life because now I do so much less work.” An executive at a food industry company remarked on “the number of people who just have thanked me because they could take a vacation.” (This is consistent with a Danish survey that found that around 10% of employees who save time with AI chatbots say they take more breaks or have more leisure time.) But some managers were less enthused. One frustrated executive described his employees as hiding their AI-enabled successes, saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.” A private equity manager suspected that, among workers at companies in his portfolio, “some of them are working basically half days.”.

Our interviews show substantial variation in the degree and kind of value companies derive from AI. The highest-value applications involve wide-reaching organizational change. These patterns warrant attention to the specifics of AI deployments across these companies. In the following section, we assess three common adoption strategies that we observed in our interviews: top-down automation, bottom-up experimentation, and a broader reorganization around AI.

According to recent reports, mark racked his brain: had he messed anything up recently? As a paralegal at his law firm, he was rarely called into a partner’s office and even more rarely ended up in an office with two of the firm’s equity partners. They wanted to “talk about his AI use,” a topic that filled him with dread. He had already realized that models’ continued improvement would mean “the beginning of the end for my work.” He worried, “Why would anyone want to employ someone like me?”.

Recent findings suggest that mark’s fears were understandable—and far from unique. This past year, AI has loomed especially large in performance assessments across industries. Some of the most sobering moments in our interviews were when managers described making difficult decisions to terminate employees who wouldn’t adopt AI. One engineering leader described experiencing a “morale hit” after the organization terminated a developer who, they mentioned, “just kind of shut down instead of trying to embrace it.” As one person at a financial services firm said of their company’s AI push, “You either get on board or don’t. And this might not be the place for you [if you don’t].” An engineering executive described grappling with the massive performance differences he saw emerging between AI users and AI resisters. Ultimately, he said, “we had a couple people who started off extremely anti-AI, and they moved a little along the spectrum, but not enough, and so we ended up letting them go.” But even heavy AI users were not immune to fears of losing their jobs or falling behind: one operations manager said she woke at 3 a.m., fearing for her career, and asked Claude, “How do I make sure I set myself apart so that AI can’t do everything that I do?”.

These cases were rare. Overall, people at five companies described pushing out employees who would not adopt AI, and only two had seen AI automation fully eliminate a position and lead to someone losing their job. (By contrast, 10 companies reported hiring more due to AI, primarily into AI implementation roles and to bolster IT support, and others had grown rapidly for a variety of business reasons.) But layoffs weren’t the only adverse employment effect. People at two-thirds of the companies we spoke to reported reduced hiring due to AI: as one person put it, “We may not be firing, but we’re not hiring.” A third of these hiring declines were due to companies actively shrinking functions through attrition without backfilling the roles. But most were the result of companies forgoing hiring that, in the absence of AI, they would have needed to scale their businesses—a finding consistent with past work suggesting that AI-native startups employ fewer workers. As an engineering leader at a health management company put it, “We’ve added a lot of capacity by buying tokens instead of hiring people.”.

Recent findings suggest that beyond terminations and reduced hiring, nine companies described cutting contracted software developers, customer service representatives, legal counsel, and a range of back-office functions, many of which they had already offshored. These outsourced jobs, which are based on modular tasks (self-contained pieces of work that can be handed off separately), sometimes without high expectations for quality, have been particularly vulnerable to replacement. An executive at a firm that worked with an offshore design firm stated, “We’ve since fired them because now we can get better quality things faster and cheaper” with AI. A finance company downsized well over 100 offshore data and developer contractors. An operations leader at a software company explained that with AI-driven contract reviews, their “legal bill has just completely disappeared.”.

Industry observers note that these reductions were often the result of top-down workflow automation. For example, one financial technology company adopted AI customer service agents and cut its offshore customer service contracts. Instead of managing human customer service representatives and fielding escalated calls themselves, customer service managers now review transcripts of conversations with the AI agents and edit the agents’ prompts, knowledge graphs, and general operating procedures. One company built an agent as part of a document review workflow. The agent reads submissions against the company’s approval policies and passes a structured analysis to human reviewers. Deploying the agent led the company to cut the number of reviewers it expected to hire for the coming year by more than 90%.

These agentic automations—in which AI agents are given instructions and then operate largely autonomously—are more advanced than the chatbots that still define many employees’ experiences with AI. AI-native startups take these automated workflows to the extreme, both in the products they offer and in how they organize their own work. One Chief Operating Officer walked us through his one-stop agentic portal for operations, noting that 90% of his operations budget was spent on AI tokens and 10% on headcount. He said of his approach, “Look, don’t hire anybody on the back office. I’m going to automate it.”.

Recent findings suggest that one AI startup founder told us bluntly that their company’s pitch was to replace the back-office workers their customers currently employed: “You’re trying to fire your [data] labelers, I guess.” A founder of a marketing startup described how their “marketing factory” had flipped from humans doing 80% of the work and AI doing 20% to the opposite. Another startup founder estimated that their company spent as much on internal AI use as on labor, and that it would need three times as many employees without AI. Overall, the six startups that gave us an estimate mentioned they would need, on average, four times as many employees without AI.

According to recent reports, another top-down deployment involves using AI to monitor employees more closely. Under the Anthropic Usage Policy, employee monitoring and its scope must be disclosed to employees, and the monitoring must be limited to employers’ systems for security, safety, logistics, or compliance purposes. The policy further defines employment decisions, like evaluating an employee’s performance, as high-risk, and requires a human in the loop and disclosure to employees. The workplace monitoring we heard about appeared to be compliant with these restrictions, and did not always involve Claude.

One engineering executive explained, “You want to make your work legible to your manager. But nowadays I think you want to make your work legible to the agents your manager uses.” This executive, and others we spoke to, were ambivalent about the implications of these capabilities, seeing both the benefits of more accurate performance feedback and the risks of workplace surveillance—a “panopticon effect,” as one executive put it. An operations supervisor mentioned he started each day by reviewing an AI report on the throughput and error rate of each member of his 12-person document extraction team: “If somehow there was a lag, then I can question back to them, ‘Okay, what happened this hour?’” Another operations director set up an AI-based assessment process for the firm’s customer service representatives. An agent codes their transcripts according to dozens of performance dimensions, then routes the results to a dashboard monitored by the customer service representatives’ managers.

Top-down deployments like these shift power from employees to executives and owners. But they can also be brittle, because they can promptly become out of date or obsolete. For example, the dozens of performance dimensions that customer service representatives were rated on are scored by a two-year-old model and are not taken seriously by managers. Similarly, a law firm built a series of automations for document management but ended up with a number of low-quality “zombie” apps that were hardly used. One engineering leader described a chatbot their manufacturer had built for customer service workers—an early experiment built on an open-source chat interface—as “super basic; just chat and answer.” They noted the system was difficult to revision and maintain, and that “we haven’t spent any more time or money on it.”.

Recent findings suggest that these systems are largely built by outside vendors rather than developed directly by internal users, and are marketed as targeted solutions for a specific industry and function. In interview after interview, companies described how improvements in model capabilities rendered these products outdated. As one employee noted of one such system, “It’ll be obsolete in three months.” One executive despaired of the up-front investments needed to build top-down workflows as models rapidly improved: “It’s almost like we’re trying to throw darts at a spinning dart board.”.

Sources indicate that similar problems emerge in even the most ambitious automation attempts, those targeting knowledge work that requires deep expertise. Standing up effective workflows in these areas typically requires experts to design the agents’ prompts and evaluate their outputs. But this means experts are effectively being asked to build and maintain the very systems that could replace them. One software engineer, who we’ll call Ellen, described her first encounter with automated coding: “I don’t think that my job is secure… software engineers are going to be obsolete.” Another employee put it even more bluntly: “If I’m open to this, I’m essentially building my own coffin.”.

Managers also end up facing understandable resistance from employees. Recall the company that used AI to automate an approval workflow. It intended to double the output of expert reviewers and reduce hiring by more than 90%. The human reviewers balked. As one executive put it, “Just because [a reviewer] can now do double the amount of cases, how do you incentivize them to do double the amount of cases?” The company considered offering gift cards to get reviewers to comply. At the time of our interview, the executive noted that while some reviewers were down to two minutes of review per submission, “there’s some that are hanging out in the 10-plus minutes.”.

Likewise, recall the senior developer who’d automated one law firm’s mailroom. Fresh off that success, he told us, his COO put him on a more ambitious project: using AI to check for conflicts of interest among the firm’s prospective clients. Under the existing process, conflict staff would run a search, print out any hits, and pass “the buck right onto the attorney.” In under a week, he built a workflow that let attorneys request a check from an AI agent in plain language, which then routed the request through conflict-checking software. But the fresh workflow left it to the conflict staff to work through each potential conflict—and would often surface the types of complex and difficult conflicts that had previously been passed to the attorneys. Faced with this new work, the staff pushed back, the agent was shelved, and the firm returned to its old process.

Recent findings suggest that top-down AI deployment is already changing hiring and contracting patterns by automating whole workflows. It is also prompting resistance from experts and raising fears of workplace surveillance. That resistance can result in abandoned or fragile automations.

For many companies, the problems of layoffs or the AI panopticon haven’t really arrived. Recall Mark, the paralegal who worried for his job after being called in to meet his bosses. The meeting was not the one he expected. Mark explained to us that at the meeting, the partners noted that his demand letters were better than others’ and asked him how he'd prompted AI so effectively. Mark said he’d felt hesitant about sharing his workflows. He remembered telling them, “That’s my secret sauce. I have my own workflow, my own process, and respectfully—please, do not take this the wrong way—I do not want to share with anyone.”.

This pattern, of a few individual contributors thriving with AI, came up in many of our interviews, particularly for companies doing bottom-up deployments. Nontechnical knowledge workers with substantial expertise in a given domain often derived the highest value from such deployments. This is in line with prior research on Claude Code usage, which found that nontechnical experts had the highest task success rates. One accountant described “vibe-coding” an app that audits whether the 401(k) payments employers process actually end up in the investment fund they are intended for. This audit process requires matching payment records across dozens of different systems and providers and previously took accountants 80 hours. “I was able to show that to our team. They were like, ‘Wow, this is super cool,’” the accountant mentioned. “They looked at me and they were like, ‘You built this?’ And I was like, ‘Sort of. I told Claude what I needed to do.’”.

It has been revealed that in these cases, coding tools clearly empower domain experts. A former airport operations manager told us about building a vehicle tracking app, saying, “I was wielding AI like Excalibur.” Quality assurance supervisors at a chemical plant built an app to monitor filtration rates despite having no coding experience: “They know they’re using Python because [Claude] told them.”.

However, even the most dramatic success stories were often limited to changes that could be made from the bottom up. An employee at a manufacturing organization explained, “We’re getting just these pockets of really cool stuff that could be great for our organization, but not necessarily a way to enable everyone to use that.” Swapping out a single software tool or building a new personal productivity app can be done by ambitious individual contributors. One investment manager at a real estate firm developed a deal tracker that replaced a third-party product that cost $10,000 per year. Another created a legacy Windows XP app that would have cost $250,000 to replace.

While many of these homegrown software replacements seem like notable upgrades at first, they still require review and ongoing maintenance—which means they can result in relatively small savings overall. How customized (and, therefore, how complex) does a deal tracker really need to be? An operations director at a large law firm considered building out dashboards to monitor their recruitment pipeline, but realized:.

Likewise, an engineer at a government services firm considered using AI to customize their software but decided that even if it helped them win a few contracts, “we don’t think it’s super sustainable from the maintenance and support side still. It just requires a lot of staffing.”.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3 summarizes the 140 pieces of software that interviewees described as being built with AI, broken down by the software’s purpose and the role of the person who worked with AI to build it. It reveals that product features and technical infrastructure remain solidly within the purview of technical employees, while nontechnical employees focus on internal apps and dashboards. This implies that the bulk of software built by nondevelopers still requires support or infrastructure from technical employees.

Industry observers note that beyond maintenance, these one-off, bottom-up coding projects can create substantially more work elsewhere in the organization, either in the last mile of production or through uneven acceleration across different tasks. The 401(k) audit app prototype mentioned above had to be implemented by a third-party vendor and was still not in active use months later. An engineer at an equipment manufacturer realized that AI could translate the text on their product surfaces into 10 different languages, but “we don’t have anybody that can answer the phone in those languages… So we ended up turning that [feature] off. We didn’t even ship it.” As coding accelerates relative to other functions, it hits bottlenecks: “Without the proper scaffolding in place, that bottleneck is immediate.”.

These uneven changes in productivity can also run into organizational politics. As one manager put it, “In our world, it’s like Billy in Sales doesn’t trust Sally in Marketing.” Exacerbating these conflicts is the fact that the uneven adoption of AI can impose costs on nonadopters. Power users lob “Claude grenades” and shoot “Claude cannons” at the rest of the organization, while AI skeptics respond, “Guys, I’m not reading your AI email.” In one case, an AI agent put together a set of profit and loss projections that a Chief Investment Officer realized were based on outdated assumptions. As one frustrated executive put it, “A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society.”.

Figure 4 summarizes the bottlenecks to deriving value from AI discussed across the interviews. Many involve the uneven acceleration of tasks. The difficulty of reviewing AI outputs came up again and again, as their volume swamped scarce human attention. In one incident, an agent added an errant “S” to an API endpoint and broke a carefully planned feature release. In other cases, when coding accelerated, other functions could not keep up. Uneven employee adoption was also common, as the enthusiasm of power users failed to rub off on their peers. Companies also often noted that they lacked the necessary context and infrastructure to support AI-generated software. By contrast, customer skepticism and regulation were rarely cited as bottlenecks. The bulk of bottlenecks appear to emerge from the process of adopting AI within the organization itself.

Industry observers note that these examples evoke Paul David’s mill buildings retrofitted with electric engines—a classic account of why productivity growth may lag technological implementation. Individual contributors can only revamp processes and decisions within their own small corners of an organization, while the broader division of labor remains in place. As one hotel services operations director put it, “The individual doesn’t have the authority to change the work. They can only apply it in their own area.” The head of AI at an investment firm voiced similar frustration with the bottom-up projects he had seen: “How can we upskill and tear down our workflows and rebuild like we were starting the manufacturer again now?… Not ‘Claude, write the email,’ but, ‘Why are you even getting the email?’”.

Recent findings suggest that one manager described the challenge of using AI agents to automate production planning. Setting output targets required input from a half-dozen functions spanning procurement, logistics, manufacturing, sales, and planning: “They’ve done a poor job at defining who has accountability and authority to make decisions.” The manager noted that only executive pressure could force change: “Getting them to imagine doing their job differently… can’t come from them. It has to come top-down.”.

According to recent reports, what is the alternative? Can AI deployment avoid both brittle automation of low-value tasks and the bottleneck of hobbyist projects the organization can’t absorb? Mark, the paralegal, ultimately agreed to share his approach with the partners and the rest of his firm. He had effectively automated the most relaxed part of his job—firing off AI-written demand letters. But he gained a new responsibility: supporting his firm’s AI transition and enablement.

Sources indicate that some companies are experimenting with complementary organizational changes in response to AI rather than just automating existing workflows or handing out AI tools. Here, we look at three ways companies have pursued these organizational changes: broadening roles to reduce coordination costs, redeploying employees toward “bottleneck” tasks, and building common infrastructure to support nontechnical builders.

When firms broaden employees’ roles, individuals become responsible for an entire workflow rather than one narrow type of expertise. Engineers, for example, might start working across product, design, and even customer engagement. One healthcare startup asked all of its engineers—not just its business people—to speak regularly to medical professionals who used their product. Having a single employee or small team own an entire product or customer relationship limits the organizational friction and potential vetoes that can otherwise block AI acceleration. As one engineering leader put it, “Two people plus Claude is the most amazing thing… if two people agree on something, just ship it.”.

As production—not just of code but also of legal research, data analysis, financial modeling, and other aspects of knowledge work—speeds up, agreeing on what to build across the organization can become slow and costly. But the more a single individual or a small team controls an entire workflow, the less these coordination costs appear. One executive described rethinking their lead sourcing, account executive, and customer success roles, merging them into a single role that handles the whole customer life cycle. AI tools made keeping up with the details of each step in the deal process easier, and made the “context loss” associated with handing a task off to a colleague more costly. One startup founder described exclusively employing individual contributors and giving each of them ownership over a distinct part of the product and business. At another organization, a manager explained that “we essentially collapse designer, product manager, engineer, and QA, and even infrastructure, into a singular role.” Another engineering leader aimed at “more full-body contact of engineers with customers.” Figure 5 highlights examples of roles broadening from specific functions to whole workflows.

Sources indicate that another benefit of role broadening is that even as some parts of a job are automated, experts have less reason to fear job loss. At current model capabilities, agentic workflows still typically need active expert engagement and input to develop. They also require ongoing maintenance as models improve and workflows change. For example, one engineer automated a system to respond to production-alert tickets, which had previously been a substantial part of his job. For two months after deploying the system, the engineer read transcripts of every conversation with the AI agent and tweaked the prompts, repaired broken integrations, supplied missing vendor documentation, and approved agents’ authorization requests. Six months in, with the system working well, he still sampled transcripts every two weeks to patch and maintain the system. He also kept building on it. The alert agent became a firm-wide Slack agent (“the company basically runs on it now”), and then an agent that keeps skills and context up to date on everyone’s laptop.

According to recent reports, some companies have also found creative ways to transfer employees to new roles and build their expertise. A financial services firm, for example, shifted its internship program away from its immediate business needs toward helping interns develop domain expertise, such that now the “sole purpose is to build expertise and domain knowledge for that person.”.

It has been revealed that some companies respond to AI-enabled acceleration by shifting employees toward the tasks that are still bottlenecks. If employees can chase down bottlenecks, they can better complement the capabilities of AI models. Recall Ellen, the software engineer who was initially afraid she would lose her job to coding agents. She eventually accepted that “the entire job has switched right from writing code to making decisions.” At a consulting company, consultants helped automate the process of reconciling best practices and standards documents that conflicted with one another. The consultants then shifted to more “person-to-person consulting work instead of sifting through documents.” Likewise, an engineering director suggested that their team spend more time “talking to your PM [product manager] and helping your PM raise relevant questions against the user journey.” An operations leader noted automation gave them “more time for the process change and the buy-in. Honestly, that is the biggest battle—that process change.” In these cases, the work shifted toward the interpersonal and strategic tasks that limit models’ productivity.

Industry observers note that as another example, project managers at a construction company contributed to an agentic workflow for checking in across construction sites. Previously, project managers would call crew members at different sites every morning, put notes together, and write up a daily report for customers. Now, an AI agent pings crew members, who “talk to the robot” instead. The agent synthesizes the responses, reviews previous reports, drafts a newly introduced one, and sends it to the customer. Project managers said they got their mornings back to talk to customers about more pressing needs: “an excellent customer experience—that’s number one.” Similarly, one CTO shifted his product managers’ focus to aspects of the role that require more taste, or the ability to identify product-market fit. As the CTO put it, “Claude is a terrible product manager... So it’s a lot of taste deciding what features are notable.”.

For engineers, code review became a critical bottleneck, so many of them have worked on solving it. One engineer explained, “You find a bottleneck. Find out how to tackle that. Have someone own that. …Code’s no longer the problem. Let’s put time in user experience testing. Let’s put time in requirements gathering.” Some companies worked on automating code review, while others expanded the share of time engineers spent reviewing code. One company abandoned formal code review altogether but had developers work side by side with Claude to assess code.

The pressure to flexibly shift toward bottlenecks is especially strong with AI, because the models improve too fast for any fixed organizational proposal to keep pace. As one HR manager put it, “You wait three months, and something latest you didn’t think AI could do is now possible. And you’re like, ‘Well, okay, let me revise my whole plan.’” A CTO said, “If the world could just pause for a minute and let us get some harnesses in place, that would be great.” AI adoption benefits from scaffolding that makes role changes easier as the bottlenecks keep moving.

Figure 6 shows what these role changes look like across a variety of jobs. As software development becomes the purview of a whole gamut of nontechnical functions, engineers broaden their scope across design, product management, and even core business functions. At the same time, fresh tasks emerge: certified public accountants grade an AI finance agent’s outputs; marketing executives edit branding skill prompts; IT decides which nondeveloper apps to put into production; a client experience manager builds synthetic customers to pitch ideas to. Production planners, accustomed to poring over spreadsheets, become data labelers, providing qualitative context for AI agents to better understand the numbers: “You should be a journalist… you should not think about competing with AI.”.

Representatives at the largest firms we interviewed remarked they were systematically inventorying employees’ skills and tracking shifts in their labor needs to formalize these changes. At one HR support firm, an agentic workflow automated the work of a team that had assessed clients’ employees for benefits eligibility. The team pivoted to client-facing work, answering calls and providing high-touch customer support, which the organization had not previously had the resources to do. At a construction company, a contract administrator helped automate their own data-gathering work and was redeployed to integrate AI across the company and maintain agentic workflows. Redeployments like these can keep automation from leading to layoffs.

Several companies have set up common infrastructure that allows nontechnical people to build apps that do not expose security vulnerabilities or require substantial maintenance by engineers. “Every single employee now is a developer… creating additional attack surface every day,” a data security executive told us. The head of engineering at a real estate company stated they “went from having a team of five developers to a team of [dozens of] developers that all want to release software.”.

Sources indicate that perhaps the most vital shared infrastructure is firm data, which provides context both for increasingly autonomous agents and for employees across functions. With AI, an executive can query business data “at the moment of need” rather than waiting for a regular report from data analysts. A trucking company built an agent-accessible “data warehouse,” and managers across the company began creating their own analyses based on that data: “they’re absolutely addicted to it,” a person at the company said. Instead of a business intelligence or data science team mediating every request for analysis—“it would have ended up on the queue, sometimes a year or two”—a broad range of knowledge workers started running SQL queries themselves. At another company, a sales team leapt into data analysis, linking sales and finance data: “Anybody can do it. And so now everybody does it.” Without AI, one employee said, “they probably would have never seen [the data], or they would have never tried to do anything with it.” And the trust and safety team at an online marketplace used their fresh data analytics tools to identify fraud patterns. As one team member explained, “we can [now] go parse through all of our logs.” These examples all depended on companies first pulling in and consolidating their data so that AI had the context it needed. This is consistent with prior research on enterprise use, which found that more complex tasks tend to require more context from users (measured in input tokens).

In a recent development, making data available to the whole organization can shift power downward. As one executive put it, “You have to trust the democratization of data.” At one company, the reporting team initially protested: “Hey, we have to stop Claude from accessing data. People are reporting on things that we normally report on.” But the AI advocates won out, and the work of the reporting and business intelligence teams changed. Rather than creating reports and building dashboards, the teams were able to offer advice and insight derived from more rapid and sophisticated analysis.

According to recent reports, for AI-native startups, a structured pool of data is critical. Teams transcribe and graph customer calls and pull meeting transcripts into Slack and other public surfaces: “We just, like, transcribe everything.” An AI lead at an investment firm described urging employees to move out of direct messages and “work out loud.”.

Sources indicate that the same data and AI tooling can give executives more oversight of employees and give employees more leverage in the organization. Prior research has found that information technologies tend to push decision-making down to employees, while communication technologies tend to centralize it. Our interviews suggest that how organizations set up AI tools, such as who can access data, can tilt a given technology toward empowering employees.

It has been revealed that the dozens of people we interviewed told us that AI has substantially automated a range of work at their companies, particularly in software engineering, customer service, and back-office roles. But we also heard about a variety of bottlenecks that prevented productivity gains on particular tasks from translating into overall benefits for businesses. As one executive put it, “The closer you are to the money, the harder it is for models to excel in that job.” If prototyping is fast but deployment is not, or production is fast but marketing is slow, then AI tools deliver far less than model evaluations and capabilities would imply.

Industry observers note that the people working alongside AI face even deeper problems. In top-down deployments, automation and surveillance threaten to undermine employees. In bottom-up deployments, inconsistent velocity across the organization leads to inequality in performance between employees or teams.

Companies that reorganized around AI addressed the challenges associated with both top-down and bottom-up approaches. Developers broadened their remit across the full software stack, then shifted toward product, design, and quality assurance. Nontechnical employees found themselves needed for a whole range of novel tasks. The underlying approach was to shift people’s jobs toward the tasks that AI can’t yet accomplish. Broadening jobs also gave the people closest to the work the authority to redesign their workflows. And shared data and infrastructure helped knowledge workers collaborate with AI, extending the benefits of coding agents beyond engineers.

Recent findings suggest that our interviews suggest a path that could benefit both employees and employers. Given current model capabilities, experts are still critical to building and reviewing AI workflows. Interpersonal and strategic tasks are right now the central bottlenecks where humans are needed, but the details of these roles will continue to change as models improve. Employers that develop systems to redeploy employees in upcoming roles and broaden their scope may be best placed to take advantage of these intelligence gains without displacing employees.

How can employers deliver on this potential? Our interviews suggest that some companies are already sharing the gains of AI deployments with their employees, using productivity gains to improve job quality and lighten tedious work. Sharing the gains in this way may also motivate employees to contribute their expertise to redesigning workflows for AI tools. Companies that commit to internal worker reallocation must proposal ahead for where those workers could go. And they can give employees, including nontechnical ones, broad access to the data and infrastructure they need to make the most of newly introduced AI tools. Finally, model developers like Anthropic must support these practices by offering training and help to business customers. We hope the findings in this report will inform those efforts.

It has been revealed that none of this is a guarantee against AI-induced job loss, and it will not replace a strong policy response in the event of substantial technological disruption. But the wide variation in how employers are deploying the same technology suggests they have some say in how AI changes work.

For technical details on the study, see the Appendix in our report PDF. The PDF also contains a full list of the sources used in this research.

01Note that a given use case can be attributed different degrees of value and come with different levels of organizational change in different companies. Coding agents for frontend development, for example, can supercharge product development at one organization and degrade the codebase at another.

We are grateful to the Anthropic customers who took the time to talk candidly with us about how they are implementing AI. For very helpful comments and assistance, we thank Kia Amiri, Scott Booth, Keir Bradwell, Yena Cho, Brian Clarke, Eleanor Dorfman, Adam Farina, Rebecca Hiscott, Hanah Ho, Tyler Kivley, Caitlin Love, Kerry Persen, Celeste Ridlen, Szymon Sacher, David Saunders, Carolyn Stein, Monika Tuchowska, Scott White, Heather Whitney, and Kim Withee. For help facilitating interviews, we thank Nanita Balagopal, Craig Barry, Alyssa Bonadies, Carolyn Briggs, Travis Bryant, Emily Cole, Tania Ehrsam, Maddie Field, Emily Gray, Bets Hudson, Don Hutchinson, Kelly Kevin, Bill Kolman, Kelly Loftus, Brian Malconian, Katie McNamara, Cope Ono, Camy Pearson, Dartagnan Phan, Naresh Pillay, Meghana Reddy, Conrad Sager, Gurneev Sareen, Lucy Stebbins, Chase Taylor, Michael Taylor, Drew Visconti, Josh Walden, and Robby Weitzman.

Recent findings suggest that aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

According to recent reports, it was a shame because in that cameo, Fernandes showed he has returned from the World Cup in excellent shape, the tempo of United’s play immediately lifting when he had the ball. It is wrong to make conclusions in the summer, but you are on safe ground to state he will be integral to their ambitions.

Croke Park is a stadium steeped in history and another chapter was penned here, as the capacity crowd made this the highest attended soccer match in Ireland with 82,000 coming through the gates: it is a magnificent venue, one that would be well capable of hosting a Champions League final.

Michael Carrick hopes in years to come that is the stage where his team will be but, right now, it is a case of learning to walk again before they can run and he more than anyone will know how far off that target is, not that it will stop him trying to get there.

The one thing that is obvious about the way United play under him is the first thought from everyone is to go forward rapidly. Yes, this was only a friendly, but the ambition to be on the front foot and cause problems was evident from the start.

The team in red had much the better of the opening exchanges, with Diogo Dalot having the first shot that went over but, unlike on July 25, when Mayo beat Kerry here in Gaelic football’s All Ireland final, which went viral, nobody was cheering the sight of a ball clearing the bar.

It was like a home game for United and the majority got what they wanted in the 15th minute when a slick counter-attack ended with Bryan Mbuemo sliding a pass into Joshua Zikzee, who rifled past James Trafford with a first-time finish.

Recent findings suggest that devastating counterattack! 💥Manchester United break and Joshua Zirkzee is there to finish it off 🤩 pic.twitter.com/y6QHbZMi7n.

Zirkzee is unlikely to be part of Carrick’s squad beyond the transfer window, with interest from clubs in Italy, and it would be disingenuous to suggest his career at Old Trafford has been successful, but his attitude was exemplary and he played as if he was desperate to change his manager’s mind.

There may have been an anticipation that United would stride clear, but this game was also about Leeds, whose summer has been encouraging and whose confidence from staying up last season has evidently enabled them to blossom.

You would be way off the mark if you include them in your conversations about which clubs are going to be relegated next May, and the sense they revealed to stay with Daniel Farke has paid off. They have bought some good players, not least goalkeeper James Trafford and Harry Wilson.

Top stop from James Trafford! 🚫The Leeds United keeper has been busy in the first half... pic.twitter.com/VKmxNVKBsA.

Trafford has done the right thing getting away from Manchester City and you could argue that he is already reaping the benefit of playing for a manager who wants him, as he made a fabulous save in the 23rd minute to thwart Mbuemo. It was all part of performance that led to him being named player of the match.

He was involved in the move that brought the Leeds equaliser, too, as his long clearance caused uncertainty and led to Tyler Fletcher being pickpocketed by Dan James and he nudged a pass into Brenden Aaronson, who kept his cool and danced into the area, ignoring Senne Lammens, to finish.

Recent findings suggest that leeds hit back with their first shot on target! 💥Brenden Aaronson with a cool finish 🥶 pic.twitter.com/5WsSZY41j6.

In a recent development, it was an entertaining affair, mercifully lacking the bile that would usually bubble away when it is staged in England, and the longer the game advanced, the better Leeds looked. They finished the opening period strongly and came back after the restart, with 10 changes, in the same fettle.

Farke, whose team had shown their ability to score heavily when they pummelled Liverpool 4-2 in Chicago 10 days ago, would have taken plenty of encouragement, but the perfectionist in him would have cursed the opportunities that were squandered early in the second period.

The misses proved costly as the game meandered and the shoot-out went United’s way, after Wilson and James Justin failed from 12 yards, with Noussair Mazraoui thumping in the decisive kick. It really is never dull.

Industry observers note that good evening and welcome to live coverage of the pre-season friendly between Manchester United and Leeds United at a sold-out Croke Park in Dublin. Last year Leeds played Milan in the Irish capital and drew a crowd of 52,000 but at the GAA citadel, as I think I’m contractually obliged to call it, there will be 83,000 present, a testament to the Premier League’s reach and these two clubs’ popularity in Ireland founded on the exploits of Billy Whelan, Noel Cantwell, Johnny Giles, Roy Keane, Gary Kelly et al. It’s the first club match ever held at the stadium.

It’s a fixture that always stirs the blood and whenever it comes around you can guarantee that there will be reams of stuff about the War of the Roses, clash in styles, Busby and Revie, Bobby and Jack, large swathes of which this author has been guilty of producing. I’ll spare you all that today because while it’s relevant to fans of both clubs, they know it backwards. And it’s a match that has come around a wee bit too frequently in pre-season recently, first in Perth, Western Australia, in 2019 when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s side beat Marcelo Bielsa’s 4-0, then in 2023 in Oslo when Erik ten Haag’s second or third string defeated Daniel Farke’s threadbare, just relegated squad 2-0 and last year in Stockholm, which ended in a 0-0 draw between two scratch sides.

It has been revealed that this one comes round later in the pre-season schedule than those three so we can expect to see stronger XIs, at least for part of the game. Leeds’ pre-season has gone well: after a 3-2 defeat by Wrexham in Tampa, they have beaten Sunderland in New Jersey, Liverpool in Chicago and RB Leipzig at Elland Road. Manchester United also lost to Wrexham (in Helsinki) then beat Rosenborg in Trondheim, Atlético in Stockholm and drew one apiece with the European champions, PSG, in Gothenburg last time out.

While Leeds will have new signing James Trafford available and Noah Okafor, who scored twice in Leeds’ first league victory at Old Trafford for 45 years last April, in the squad for the first time after the World Cup, Manchester United have Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford back in training since the start of the week but it seems too soon for them to start but Youri Tielemans is pushing to make his first start.

Recent findings suggest that walmart appears to have dropped support for Apple Pay on its website and in its iPhone app. This comes just a few weeks after the retailer finally added support for Apple’s payment platform to its app and website.

In a recent development, 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

It has been revealed that appleosophy spotted the change last week. There’s no indication whether the feature was removed deliberately or if this is some sort of bug.

In the “Payment method” section of the checkout page on Walmart’s app and website, it no longer lists Apple Pay as an accepted payment method where it previously did. Not only that, but it doesn’t show up under the “Other ways to pay” or “More ways to pay” sections of the checkout page either.

Walmart still accepts Apple Pay in its retail stores. The retailer began rolling out contactless payment support in August, including Apple Pay, Google Pay, contactless cards, and more. For years, Walmart refused to support Apple Pay, instead trying (and failing) to convince shoppers to use its own Walmart Pay platform.

Industry observers note that we’ll update this post if Walmart comments on Apple Pay’s disappearance from its website and app. Hopefully, it’s a bug that the firm fixes sooner rather than later.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google is rolling out fresh privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.
  • Sources indicate that upgrade 11/24: This fresh setting is now widely rolling out.
  • Sources indicate that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the newly introduced “Chat content including text & attachments” setting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out fresh privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.

Sources indicate that upgrade 11/24: This fresh setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Sources indicate that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the newly introduced “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”.

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

According to recent reports, this is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI customers on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:.

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”.

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, owners, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”.

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “fresh settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying consumers via email.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, it retains the previous release’s 5.9 GB model footprint while significantly improving the capabilities developers need to build agents that work with private files and tools on-device. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads.

With Ternary Bonsai 2 27B, we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately.

It has been revealed that agentic workflows are particularly sensitive to model degradation: small errors can compound across successive tool calls and derail an entire task. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 significantly narrows the performance gap to the full-precision base model while retaining its compact footprint. Preserving this behavior through longer tasks is an notable milestone in improving the intelligence density of models.

We evaluated Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B against both Ternary Bonsai 2 27B and the full-precision Qwen 3.8 27B base model, as reported in the full whitepaper. We see marked improvements in agentic execution, coding, and multi-turn tool use, as shown in the table below.

On a single NVIDIA H100, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieves a generation speed of 291 tokens/s with MTP and processes a 2,000-token prompt at 3,200 tokens/s. Even on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, it delivers 204 tokens/s with MTP and a prompt processing speed of approximately 3,060 tokens/s. The demos below follow complete local workflows, from the initial request through intermediate decisions to the final result.

According to recent reports, for products, this creates room to build assistance directly into the applications where work already happens: a coding assistant working through challenges in a private repository, a document application that prepares reviewable summaries, or a desktop assistant that handles recurring analysis. Local deployment lets those products process sensitive material on the user’s device. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B strengthens the model capabilities behind that experience while keeping the compact footprint that makes it practical.

Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Apple devices (Mac, iPhone, iPad) via MLX.

Model weights are available today under the Apache 2.0 License.

Full technical details of our compression, evaluation, and benchmarking processes are available in our whitepaper.

Sources indicate that we work with teams to tailor Bonsai models to their applications, from post-training on domain-specific data to optimizing inference for target hardware. If you’re building AI products with tight memory, latency, or power requirements, we’d love to explore how Bonsai can help. Reach out at sales@prismml.com.

According to recent reports, if you've been thinking about picking up a Bluetooth tracker to keep tabs on your keys, luggage, or other valuables, now is probably the best time to get one. Apple rolled out its second-generation AirTag 2 earlier this year, but the tracker is already down to its lowest price yet for Black Friday. You can now grab a single Apple AirTag for just $18 at Amazon, down from its usual $29 price.

It has been revealed that and if you're an Android user, there's a pretty good deal for you as well. The Moto Tag 2, which offers many of the same features as Apple's AirTag, is currently down to just $19 at Amazon.

Apple's latest AirTag features an improved Precision Finding range, a 50% louder speaker, and up to a year of battery life. It works seamlessly with Apple's Find My network and is now down to just $18 (38% off).

Sources indicate that the second-generation AirTag offers up to 1.5 times the Precision Finding range of its predecessor. Apple has also upgraded the built-in speaker, making it 50% louder than the original AirTag, and features a new, more distinctive chime. this makes it a lot easier to locate your belongings when they're nearby.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest reasons to get an AirTag over most other Apple Find My-compatible trackers, though, is Precision Finding. While other key finders and trackers also let you locate your belongings through the Find My app warn you if you leave something behind, the AirTag takes things a step further with its ultra-wideband (UWB) technology.

If you've misplaced your keys somewhere around the house, for example, you can simply open the Find My app on a compatible iPhone, and it'll show you exactly which direction to walk in and how far away your AirTag is — rather than just relying on a sound to locate it.

In a recent development, and if you're planning to put AirTags on multiple belongings, there's also a deal on the AirTag four-pack, which is currently down to $79 from its usual $99 price. That noted, at $18 apiece, buying four individual AirTags actually works out slightly cheaper.

According to recent reports, if you're on the Android side of things, the Moto Tag 2 is arguably one of the best alternatives to Apple's AirTag. Much like Apple's AirTag, the Moto Tag 2 features ultra-wideband technology, which means you can use precision finding on compatible Android phones to pinpoint the location of your items.

It also works with Google's Find Hub network, so you can locate your items even when they're outside your phone's Bluetooth range.

In a recent development, the Moto Tag 2 brings an AirTag-like tracking experience to Android with UWB Precision Finding, Google's Find Hub integration, over 600 days of battery life, and IP68 water resistance. It's presently down to just $19 from $30.

According to recent reports, but there are a couple of things the Moto Tag 2 does even better than Apple's AirTag. For starters, Motorola claims over 600 days of battery life, which is considerably longer than the year of battery life Apple promises. You can also use the button on the Moto Tag 2 as a remote camera shutter, which is particularly handy for taking group photos or selfies.

You also get features like left-behind notifications and an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, so you don't have to worry too much about attaching it to your backpack or other belongings you carry outdoors.

According to recent reports, on the whole, I think $20 is a pretty reasonable amount to spend on something that could save you a lot of trouble if you ever lose your keys or luggage.
